title: T1485.001 — Data Destruction - Lifecycle-Triggered Deletion
subtitle: Watch the attack unfold through the cloud control plane, and see at the same time what the SOC can observe.

steps.title: OF 8 - LEAKED ACCESS KEY
steps.caption: The attacker finds an IAM access key that a developer leaked into a public code repository. A quick test call to the cloud API works, so the key is live and trusted. Nothing in the cloud has changed yet.
steps.defender: Defender hint: Alert on GetCallerIdentity or console logins for human identities from new source addresses.

steps.title: OF 8 - ENUMERATE THE BUCKETS
steps.caption: The attacker calls ListBuckets and receives the names of all 14 buckets in the account. The data bucket and the audit log bucket are now known targets. Still nothing is changed.
steps.defender: Defender hint: A first-time ListBuckets by an identity that never does it is cheap recon evidence worth an alert.

steps.title: OF 8 - PICK THE TWO TARGETS
steps.caption: The attacker reads lifecycle and versioning settings on the two targets. They learn that versioning protects the data bucket and that the log bucket keeps one year of audit records.
steps.defender: Defender hint: GetBucketLifecycleConfiguration on a log bucket by a new identity is recon for an evidence wipe.

steps.title: OF 8 - ARM THE DATA BUCKET One PutBucketLifecycl
steps.caption: eConfiguration call arms a rule that expires every object after one day. The cloud now holds a destruction timer for the whole data bucket, and the attacker can leave the console.
steps.defender: Defender hint: Page on any lifecycle write with an expiry of one day or less that has no change ticket.

steps.title: OF 8 - ARM THE LOG BUCKET
steps.caption: The same one-day expiry rule is applied to the CloudTrail log bucket. Audit evidence is now scheduled to destroy itself, which is the cover-up half of this technique.
steps.defender: Defender hint: Any lifecycle write on a log bucket should page, because it erases the investigation trail itself.

steps.title: OF 8 - THE TIMER RUNS Twenty-four hours pass wit
steps.caption: h no attacker online. The lifecycle service quietly deletes expired objects, so the data bucket empties while the company sleeps. This is why the API call, not the deletion, is the detection moment.
steps.defender: Defender hint: Watch object counts and inventory reports on critical buckets so silent shrinkage is visible.

steps.title: OF 8 - THE SIEM CATCHES THE CALL
steps.caption: The SIEM raised an alert the moment the rule was written, because an unusual role never writes lifecycle policies. The SOC now works a destruction timer that still has hours left to run.
steps.defender: Defender hint: Correlate lifecycle writes with identity history and change tickets so unusual roles stand out.

steps.title: OF 8 - REMOVE, RESTORE, REVOKE Responders delete
steps.caption: the lifecycle rule, restore the data bucket from the cross-region replica, and revoke the leaked key. Some already-expired log objects are gone, which is exactly why the early alert matters.
steps.defender: Defender hint: After removing a malicious rule, verify object counts everywhere and rotate every credential the identity could reach.
